title: Methods: write it once, use it everywhere

steps.title: Stop repeating yourself
steps.body:
Real programs reuse logic constantly, like working out a tax, a discount or a grade. Instead of copying the same lines, you give them a name, a **method**, and call it whenever you need it.

In five minutes you’ll watch a method being called (and see Java’s *call stack* live), then write one yourself.

options.why: The second call passes a, which is already 9, so it works out 9 * 9.
Right: square(3) is 9, and square(9) is 81.
a holds what square(3) RETURNED (9), not the 3 that was passed in.
x * x multiplies x by itself; it doesn’t double it.

steps.title: How methods work
points: A method has a **name**, **parameters** (its inputs) and a **return type** (its output), e.g. `static int square(int x)`.
Calling it runs its body with the values you pass. The caller **waits**, which is why Java keeps a **call stack**.
`return` hands a value back and ends the method. A `void` method returns nothing.
Parameters are **copies** of the values passed in. Changing a parameter doesn’t change the caller’s variable.

steps.prompt: A classic trap. What does this print?

options.why: It compiles. A void method simply doesn’t return anything.
addOne got a COPY of 5 in n. It changed its copy, not count. To change count, return the new value: count = addOne(count).
n starts as a copy of count (5), not 0.
Yes. Java passes a copy of the value, so count is untouched.

steps.prompt: Your turn. Finish cube so it returns x × x × x.
steps.hint: Multiply x by itself three times.
steps.explain: `x * x * x` works for every input, including negatives: cube(-1) is -1.
